question: Suppose a number of rays parallel to the principal axis are falling on a concave mirror, then all the reflected rays will intersect:

options.text: in between the pole and infinity

solution:
The correct answer is __**at the principal focus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When parallel rays of light fall on a concave mirror, they reflect and meet at a single point known as the principal focus.
 
• This phenomenon occurs due to the converging nature of a concave mirror.
 
• The distance from the mirror's surface to this focal point is called the focal length.
 
• The principal focus is located on the principal axis of the mirror, halfway between the mirror's surface and its center of curvature.
 
• This property of concave mirrors makes them useful in applications such as telescopes, headlights, and solar furnaces.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Principal Axis**

 
 
• The principal axis is an imaginary line that passes through the center of curvature and the pole of a mirror.
 
• It is the line along which light rays parallel to it will converge or diverge after reflection.
 
 
 
• **Focal Length**
 
 
• Focal length is the distance between the pole of the mirror and the principal focus.
 
• It is denoted by the letter 'f' and is a crucial parameter in determining the mirror's reflective properties.
 
 
 
• **Center of Curvature**
 
 
• The center of curvature is the center of the sphere from which the concave mirror is a part.
 
• The distance from the center of curvature to the mirror's surface is called the radius of curvature.
 
 
 
• **Reflection of Light**
 
 
• Reflection is the phenomenon where light bounces off a surface.
 
• In concave mirrors, reflection follows the laws of reflection, where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
